title: Maritime nations warn wars, shadow fleets are eroding global shipping rules
summary: The Consultative Shipping Group's alarm over eroding maritime rules and the rise of "shadow fleets" directly threatens environmental accountability in shipping. These unregulated vessels, operating outside conventional oversight, present a significant risk for unchecked emissions and excessive HFO consumption. Without transparent data and adherence to international standards, these fleets will continue to undermine efforts to achieve global decarbonization targets and avoid FuelEU Maritime fines.
content:
Eighteen of the world’s major maritime nations have warned that the international rules underpinning commercial shipping are beginning to break down, as wars, attacks on vessels and the growth of opaque shadow fleets change the environment in which more than 80% of global trade moves.

Wars, attacks on vessels and the growth of opaque shadow fleets are changing the environment in which more than 80% of global trade moves.

The warning came from the Consultative Shipping Group, or CSG, an alliance of maritime authorities from Europe, Asia and North America. Its members collectively represent about a fifth of global shipping tonnage.

The group said the battle over the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions and the expansion of vessels operating outside conventional insurance and regulatory systems should not be treated as isolated crises.

They were not “episodic shocks” but “signals of a structural shift” in the operating environment for world trade, the CSG said.

The CSG was created to defend open access to international shipping markets. Its 18 members are Belgium, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Japan, South Korea, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Singapore, Spain, Sweden and the UK.

Denmark holds the chairmanship and secretariat.

The Danish Maritime Authority describes the group’s core purpose as protecting “open and unimpeded access” to shipping markets. It also seeks to counter discriminatory or restrictive maritime measures.

In September 2025, the CSG called for the preservation of a rules-based maritime order and warned against protectionism and regionalization.

That concern has since become considerably less theoretical.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen sharply amid fighting involving Iran and the US. Only seven commodity vessels were recorded crossing the strait on Monday, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters.

Before the war, daily traffic was many times higher.

Some vessels may be travelling with tracking systems disabled, meaning the observed count could understate actual movements.

The 10-day average recently fell to about 10 commodity ships a day, its lowest since May. The decline came after attacks involving US and Iranian forces spilled directly into commercial shipping.

The deterioration challenges a basic assumption that has underpinned international commerce for decades. Commercial ships have generally been able to pass through international sea lanes regardless of political disputes between surrounding countries.

International Maritime Organization rules cover ship safety, security, construction, operations and environmental standards.

The UN agency says a safe and predictable global regulatory framework is essential because international shipping carries more than 80% of global trade.

Shadow fleet creates parallel shipping system

The second concern is the rapid expansion of the so-called shadow fleet. These are largely older tankers used to transport oil affected by sanctions on countries including Russia and Iran.

Such vessels often have opaque ownership and may change flags or identities. They can operate with limited scrutiny and, in some cases, rely on insurance outside the established Western protection and indemnity system.

Industry estimates cited by the Financial Times put the shadow tanker fleet at more than 1,500 vessels.

Reuters has separately reported that hundreds of such ships are transporting sanctioned Iranian and Russian oil with limited insurance, safety checks or regulatory scrutiny.

The problem goes beyond sanctions enforcement. Part of the global fleet operates under established insurance, environmental, transparency and safety standards. Another part increasingly operates outside them.

The result is effectively a two-tier maritime system.

The CSG says the answer is not simply to write more rules. It wants existing international rules enforced more consistently across jurisdictions and governments to cooperate more closely on free navigation and fair competition.

The stakes extend well beyond shipowners.

UN Trade and Development says maritime transport carries more than 80% of goods traded worldwide by volume. It connects raw-material suppliers, factories and consumer markets. Disruption at major sea lanes can quickly feed into freight costs, energy prices, food supplies and manufacturing chains.

Recent crises at the Suez Canal, Panama Canal, Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz have shown how disruptions at narrow maritime chokepoints can force ships onto longer routes and raise transport costs.
